title: Forgiveness and Repair
verse: “But with you there is forgiveness, so that we can, with reverence, serve you.”
context: Read Psalm 130:3-4 together. The prayer imagines the weight of a record of wrongdoing, then turns toward forgiveness and a renewed relationship with God.
word_note: Selichah is a noun: forgiveness. In the verse, ha-selichah includes ha-, the definite article. Salach is the related verb: to forgive. Keep the grammar distinct from the interpretation: the word does not itself mean forgetting, erasing, or rebuilding trust.

readings.heading: 1. What has changed in Judah?
readings.text: Judah once proposed selling Joseph. Years later, he offers to become a slave so that Benjamin can go home. Compare the two choices. Rabbi Jonathan Sacks reads Judah’s reversal through Maimonides’ account of repentance: faced with the chance to repeat a wrong, a changed person acts differently.

readings.heading: 2. Why is repayment not enough?
readings.text: Maimonides says that someone who has wronged another must restore what is owed and seek that person’s forgiveness. Even after repaying money, there is a person to approach. Repair has a practical part and a personal part.

questions: What makes Judah’s later choice more persuasive than an apology alone? What would changed behavior look like in an ordinary disagreement?
Why might someone still need an apology after a debt is repaid? Name one thing an apology can acknowledge that money cannot.
closing: For reflection: What can I put right before I ask to be forgiven?

further_reading.author: Rabbi Jonathan Sacks
further_reading.title: The Birth of Forgiveness
further_reading.note: A reading of Joseph, Judah, and the possibility of becoming a different person.
